passage:
Gurleen had opened her acceptance mail at nineteen and felt no joy at all, only a flicker of dread. At the institute, her batch-mates talked about summer research and famous mentors. She told her friend Abhinav, "They'll realise soon that they picked the wrong file." When he said her project was the best in the lab, she answered, "The topic was easy." Every night she compared her notes with theirs and saw only the gaps.
At twenty-four, she began at a logistics firm. In Monday meetings, colleagues spoke with easy certainty, and Gurleen sat with a pen and an unread list of thoughts. Inside she was full of questions. Outside, everyone else looked sure. She said nothing week after week. When a new client project was assigned, the manager gave it to Joseph, who had spoken up about a route problem that Gurleen had also noticed. Gurleen looked at her notebook. "See? Nobody thinks I add much," she thought. She did not notice that nobody had heard what she thought in the first place.

qa.q: Who did the manager give the new client project to?
qa.a: The manager gave it to Joseph, who had spoken up about a route problem.

qa.q: How does Gurleen's habit at the logistics firm connect to how she felt at the institute?
qa.a: At the institute she compared her notes with theirs and saw only the gaps. At the firm she compared her inside questions with everyone else's sure manner and stayed silent, and the silence made her less visible, which fed her belief that she added little.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when she said nothing in Monday meetings?
qa.a: She felt insecure and doubtful, thinking everyone else was sure while she was only full of questions.

qa.q: What could Gurleen do to make herself heard in meetings?
qa.a: She can share one point from her list each week, and ask Joseph or a trusted colleague how they decide when to speak.

grounding: Fraud feelings and harsh comparison at a top college (4092) become silence in meetings at a new job that makes the person less visible (3230): one person over years.

passage:
At five, Kiran stood at the gate of a birthday party and pressed against Mummy Damini's side. Balloons bobbed, and strangers called out hello. Kiran hid behind Mummy's dupatta and would not look up. Mummy did not pull Kiran out. She stood close, one hand on Kiran's back, until the music felt less loud.
At nine, Kiran walked into a new school for the first day of class four. The corridor was long, and voices bounced off the walls. Kiran's stomach knotted, and the heart thumped so hard it could be felt in the ears. "Something bad is going to happen," Kiran told Mummy in the doorway. "My body is telling me." Mummy Damini crouched. "Your body is sounding an alarm, but it doesn't always mean danger. Shall I walk you to the door?" At the classroom, Kamal Sir smiled and said Kiran could sit near the window. Kiran took a breath, and the thumping slowed just a little. Mummy waved from the corridor, and Kiran waved back before stepping through.

qa.q: Where did Kamal Sir say Kiran could sit?
qa.a: He said Kiran could sit near the window.

qa.q: How is Kiran's alarm at the new school related to hiding at the party?
qa.a: At five, staying near Mummy eased what scared Kiran. At nine, the knotted stomach and thumping heart felt like proof that something bad was about to happen, and Mummy's calm words and nearness again helped Kiran take a step.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when saying "Something bad is going to happen"?
qa.a: Kiran was scared and anxious, and the body's alarm felt like proof of danger.

qa.q: What could Mummy Damini do to help Kiran over the next few days?
qa.a: She can keep gentle nearness at drop-off, praise each small step, and check with the school if the worry keeps going.

grounding: A child hides behind a parent at a party (3921) and later feels an alarm in the body on the first day at a new class, taking it as proof of danger (3285).

passage:
At five, Suraj lay flat on the living-room rug ten minutes after putting away his toy cars. "I'm bored. What can I do? Can I use the tablet?" Mummy Sabina handed him a tin of odd spoons, a ball of wool and two chairs. "Make a road." Suraj sighed loudly. Then he wound the wool round the chair legs into a web and drove a spoon down it. Half the morning went by.
At nine, Suraj came in from the garden with a pot he was told to wash. "Ugh! It smells so bad." He held it at arm's length and scrunched his nose. In the evening, Asif Sir showed the class a jar of water with a pinch of salt and a paper clip on the surface. Suraj frowned, then his eyes widened. "Aha! The salt makes the water push up, so the clip floats!" He jumped up. Asif Sir clapped. "That click of understanding is what scientists love. Tell us how you worked it out." Suraj explained it in three sentences and sat down glowing.

qa.q: What did Mummy Sabina give Suraj to make a road?
qa.a: She gave him a tin of odd spoons, a ball of wool and two chairs.

qa.q: How do Suraj's sounds at nine relate to the boredom at five?
qa.a: At five his boredom became a game once he was given time and simple things. At nine, his "Ugh!" showed disgust at the smelly pot, while his "Aha!" marked a sudden click of understanding that Asif Sir celebrated.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when he said "Aha!" in Asif Sir's class?
qa.a: He felt excited and proud, because the idea suddenly made sense to him.

qa.q: What could Asif Sir do next to build on Suraj's discovery?
qa.a: He can ask Suraj to test another object in the jar, and invite him to explain his idea to the class.

grounding: A child's boredom that becomes play (4068) and a school-age child's 'ugh' at a chore and 'aha' at a discovery (2370): one boy across years.

passage:
At ten, Kishore got stuck on the word "temperature" while reading aloud. His face went hot. He stuck out his tongue, wobbled his head and read the next line like a robot. The class burst into laughter, and Kishore bowed, but his hands shook on the book.
At twenty, Kishore sat at the back of a presentation. Anjali, at the front, said "1950" when she meant "1590" and did not notice. Kishore let out a low, quiet chortle, a private little sound. Anjali heard it. Her cheeks burned, and she stopped in the middle of a sentence. Afterwards, she said to her friend Himani, "He laughed at my mistake." Himani frowned. "Maybe ask him what it meant?" Anjali found Kishore outside. "Were you laughing at me?" Kishore blinked. "No, sorry, it was relief. I made the same slip in my presentation last week, and thought I was the only one. I should have kept quiet." Anjali let out a breath. "It sounded like mocking." He nodded. "I'll be careful how I laugh," he said.

qa.q: What number did Anjali say instead of "1590"?
How do the laughter at ten and the chortle at twenty show that the same sound can mean different things?
qa.a: At ten Kishore made the class laugh with him, and it covered his shaking hands. At twenty his quiet chortle was relief, but aimed at Anjali's slip it sounded like mocking, so context decides what a laugh means.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when she stopped mid-sentence and her cheeks burned?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hurt, thinking that Kishore was laughing at her mistake.

qa.q: What did Himani do well, and what could Kishore do next time?
qa.a: Himani suggested asking what it meant instead of assuming. Kishore can keep quiet or say something kind when someone slips, so his sound is not read as mockery.

grounding: A class clown's joke covering embarrassment (3891) and, years later, a private chortle at someone's slip that could be read as mockery though it was relief (2682).
